FND01-BP02 Establish ownership for billing, security, and operations
Every resource in your workload needs a named owner so that changes,
    troubleshooting, and cost decisions have a clear point of contact.
    Assign owners for workloads, accounts, infrastructure, shared
    services, and applications. Record that ownership in a central
    register or as metadata on the resource.
Desired outcome:
Your resources have identified owners by using metadata or a
        central register.
Your AWS accounts have a single owner where possible.
You have configured alternate contacts for billing, security,
        and operations in all accounts.
Your ownership model defines risk ownership, change ownership,
        and support responsibility.
Common anti-patterns:
Leaving alternate contacts for AWS accounts unpopulated, causing
        critical notifications to be missed.
Setting the security alternate contact to a team or individual
        with no security knowledge, runbooks, or permissions to act on
        the notifications they receive, so security findings reach a
        recipient who cannot respond.
Deploying resources without tags that identify the teams that
        own them.
Routing incidents to an ITSM queue without an email mapping,
        delaying response.
Assigning two teams overlapping ownership of a critical piece of
        infrastructure, creating unclear accountability during
        incidents.
Maintaining ownership information in a document that is rarely
        reviewed or updated, leading to stale assignments.
Relying only on periodic cleanup instead of tying resource
        ownership reassignment to the HR joiner, mover, and leaver
        process, so resources owned by employees who move or leave
        linger without a current owner until the next review.
Benefits of establishing this best
    practice:
Assigned ownership makes change approvals direct and reduces
        coordination overhead.
The correct owners can be engaged quickly when troubleshooting
        issues, which minimizes downtime.
Clear ownership tracking supports accurate cost allocation and
        chargeback to the responsible cost centers.
Compliance and audit processes take less effort when ownership
        information is consistent and readily available.
Level of risk exposed if this best practice
    is not established:
High
Implementation guidance
Clear resource ownership is a foundational element of cloud
      governance because it determines accountable parties during
      changes, incidents, and cost attribution. Without defined
      ownership, organizations experience delayed incident response,
      unclear change approval processes, and difficulty tracking cloud
      spending back to responsible teams.
Ownership models typically span multiple dimensions that rarely
      align to the same team:
Risk ownership:
The team
          accountable for business consequences
Change ownership:
The team
          authorized to modify the resource
Support responsibility:
responders to pages and incidents
Financial accountability:
The cost center that pays for the resource
A single resource can have four different owners across these
      dimensions, and clarity about each dimension reduces coordination
      cost during high-stakes events.
In AWS, ownership is recorded through multiple mechanisms.
AWS Organizations
manages alternate contacts for billing,
      security, and operations across all accounts, so AWS notifications
      reach the right teams as people change roles. Account-level tags
      in AWS Organizations apply to all metered usage in the account,
      which makes them useful for cost allocation. Tags record
      resource-level ownership. Enforce them with
AWS Config rules
so the data flows into cost allocation, access
      control, and operational workflows. For services and resources
      outside AWS, a central register keeps ownership information
      accessible during incidents and audits.
These alternate contacts receive AWS security notifications,
      billing questions, and operational communications. They're
      account-level metadata, separate from your IAM users or federated
      identities. When these contacts point to people who have left the
      organization, critical notifications such as an AWS abuse report
      about unintended access can go unanswered. Alternate contacts
      route billing notifications to finance and security notifications
      to the security team, so nothing is cross-posted to a single
      inbox.
Important
Use distribution
        lists and shared phone numbers for alternate contacts rather
        than individual email addresses. People change roles and leave
        organizations, and a missed AWS security or billing notification
        can lead to unintended access or service disruption.
Use a consistent set of ownership tags (typically
      Owner, CostCenter,
      BusinessUnit, and
      Environment). These tags feed cost allocation,
      access control, automation, and incident response. Tags only work
      when they're enforced. Without enforcement, teams skip tags under
      deadline pressure or introduce variations of the same tag
      (Owner, owner,
      ownerEmail, OwnedBy) that
      break queries and reports.
Tag policies in AWS Organizations
define required tag keys and
      allowed values, and AWS Config rules detect non-compliant
      resources. Service control policies can block resource creation
      when required tags are missing. Introduce SCP-based enforcement
      carefully to avoid blocking legitimate operations.
Define the ownership model before you deploy resources. If you
      retrofit the model onto a large environment, you have to backfill
      metadata across thousands of existing resources. An informal
      handoff during a team reorganization leaves behind stale tags,
      outdated alternate contacts, and unrevised documentation, making
      ownership unclear. For non-AWS systems that interact with your
      cloud environment, maintain a current central register as the
      source of truth during incident response. Integrate it with
      runbooks and operational processes so the information stays in
      regular use.
Implementation steps
Define ownership categories for your
            organization:
Determine what ownership means for
            the resource use cases in your environment. Ownership can
            imply who owns the risk for the resource, who owns changes
            to the resource, who supports the resource when
            troubleshooting, or who is financially or administratively
            accountable. Document these categories and the specific tag
            keys that will capture them (such as
            Owner, CostCenter,
            BusinessUnit,
            Environment). Establish the process for
            transferring ownership when teams reorganize, and integrate
            it with your HR joiner, mover, and leaver workflow so that
            when an employee changes role or leaves, the resources they
            own are reassigned to a new owner or decommissioned as part
            of offboarding rather than left to be discovered later.
Configure alternate contacts using
            AWS Organizations:
Use
AWS Organizations to manage alternate contacts
for your
            accounts centrally. Use company-owned email distribution
            lists and shared phone numbers for billing, operations, and
            security contacts in each active AWS account. This approach
            provides redundancy when individuals change roles or leave
            the company. Point the security alternate contact at a team
            that has the knowledge, runbooks, and permissions to act on
            security notifications, ideally one with 24/7 coverage such
            as a security operations center (SOC), so findings reach
            responders who can investigate and remediate without delay.
            Point the billing alternate contact on each payer
            (management) account at the team that owns invoice payment,
            typically procurement or finance, so payment issues are seen
            and resolved before they escalate to account suspension. If
            an account is not managed by AWS Organizations, configure
            the account's alternate contacts directly to point to a
            group rather than an individual. Document which distribution
            list owns each contact type and establish a process for
            periodic validation that the distribution lists remain
            monitored.
Apply account-level tags in AWS Organizations:
Tag your AWS accounts with
            ownership metadata such as owner, cost center, business
            unit, or environment directly in
AWS Organizations
. Account-level tags apply to all
            metered usage within the account, which makes them useful
            for cost allocation even for resources that do not support
            resource-level tags. Activate account tags as
cost allocation tags
in the Billing and Cost Management
            console so they appear in your Cost and Usage Reports
            alongside resource-level tags. Newly activated tags can take
            up to 24 hours to appear in reports, so activate them early.
            Use account-level tags as a fallback when resource-level
            tagging is incomplete.
Implement ownership tags for AWS
            resources:
Use tags to identify owners and their
            contact information for individual AWS resources within each
            account. Use
AWS Config
rules such as
required-tags
to enforce that resources have the required ownership tags,
            and pair them with
automated remediation
for non-compliant resources. Shift
            enforcement left by validating tags in CI/CD pipelines with
            tools like
AWS CloudFormation Guard
before resources are created.
            For in-depth guidance on building a tagging strategy, see
Best Practices for Tagging AWS Resources
.
Integrate ownership data with
            operational workflows:
Configure monitoring and
            alerting systems to include ownership tags in notification
            payloads so that alerts route directly to the responsible
            team. Use
AWS Cost Anomaly Detection
to send cost alerts to the
            owners identified through cost allocation tags. Integrate
            ownership data from tags or your central register into your
            ITSM system so incidents route automatically to the correct
            support teams, and expose the same data in dashboards that
            responders use during incidents.
Document ownership for non-AWS             resources:
For other resources, services, and
            infrastructure that integrate with your cloud environment,
            create documentation that identifies ownership. Store this
            documentation in a system accessible to all team members,
            ideally integrated with your incident response runbooks so
            ownership information is available exactly when it is
            needed. Maintain the documentation as part of your
            operational processes, with a regular review cadence
            (quarterly is typical) to keep it current. Establish clear
            responsibility for who maintains the register and how
            updates are propagated.
Review accounts on a regular cadence
            and act on stale ownership:
Schedule a periodic
            review (quarterly aligns with the cadence in Step 6) that
            scans every AWS account for signals of stale or missing
            ownership: absent Owner,
            CostCenter, or
            BusinessUnit tags, alternate contacts
            that bounce or no longer point to monitored distribution
            lists, no recent
AWS CloudTrail
activity, and zero or near-zero spend.
            Enumerate accounts through the
AWS Organizations
APIs, source spend signals from
AWS Cost Explorer
, and source activity signals from
            CloudTrail. Automate the review with
AWS Lambda
on an
Amazon EventBridge
schedule that flags candidates, notifies
            the responsible team, and (after a defined holding period)
            queues approved closures. For each candidate, reassign
            ownership, repurpose the account, or queue it for closure.
            Account closure is bounded by
CloseAccount API quotas
, so the automation must rate-limit
            closures within those quotas and prefer account reuse when
            the existing structure still fits. See
FND01-BP01 Establish management account and organizational structure
for OU
            placement (such as the Suspended OU with a deny-all SCP)
            used as the staging area during the closure path.
